276.t: Nash plays old blues on guitar
276.s: Asked for the kind of blues played in Spano's or Kaiser's, Nash plays one about going to the station and the train.
276.q: Well I know, I know some old way back down the blues they used to play. Yeah, something like they would play in there.

276.t: Singing in honky-tonks and cabarets; 'Blue Every Monday'
276.s: Nash names the places he sang in and sings a blues about days of the week.
276.q: Okay, I'll play it. I don't mind. I'm blue every Monday, thinking over Sunday, that's one day when I'm with you. I sigh every Tuesday, I cry all day Wednesday, oh my, how I long for you. And then come Thursday, years long, it never goes by. Friday makes me feel like I'm going to die. I don't mind,…

276.s: Nash sings and plays a blues with the line about three women in his life, followed by instrumental guitar.
276.q: With a guitar. Is that for my beer? Yeah, that's a good one. Mm-hmm . Yeah, the sun gonna shine In my back though someday Went to the station I looked up on the boat I pray to say your good gal Have caught the train Gonna keep on drinking Trying to drive my blues away Yeah, the sun gonna shine In…

247.s: Asked who the best blues players were, he answers confusedly and the recording ends on trumpet and trombone.
247.q: How many of them did you play? How many of them did you play? Uh... I was forced to fall time, but he's dead too. How many of them did you play? Four... Four... Four...

34.t: Burns session opens: a barrelhouse piano man
34.s: Buddy Burns, in a separate session, tries to recall a barrelhouse pianist and prepares to play.
34.q: Oh, what's he called him? What do you name him? It was a bell house piano man. No, Eddie Johnson is a sax man. Talking about, you can't call his name either? He's raised up under him, he's older too. Pretty old man, if he was living, he's dead now. Yeah, he's a good feeling. Played all that.

121.s: He learned and covered a song sent from Chicago, with Ernest McClain's guitar solo, then they check the reissue album.
121.q: That was a tune, yeah. It was a tune that was sent down here for me to record by Lou Chud, I think. And we did a cover on somebody from Chicago. Who it was, I don't know.

642.t: Guesnon performs his original 'Going Home Blues' for Rolf's band
642.s: He sings his own composition as a favor for Rolf and his band in Sweden and sends greetings to a banjo player.
642.q: I'm tired of walking dusty highways, tired of having some old boxcores for my home. Oh yes, yes. I said I'm tired of walking dusty highways, tired of having some old boxcores for my home. Yes, I'm tired of being without someone to love. I'm tired of being so blue and all alone. That's why I'm…

10.t: Garbled piano playing and talk of a piece series
10.s: Carew restarts a piece at the piano (transcript garbled); they discuss a numbered series of pieces and a singer-pianist.
10.q: Let me try that again. Boy, you might as well listen to that when you're gone. Boy, you might as well listen to that when you're gone. Boy, you might as well listen to that when you're gone. Boy, you might as well listen to that when you're gone. Boy, you might as well listen to that when you're…

643.t: Attempt to get a family member to play; light and eyesight
643.s: Zander asks to hear someone play; there is hesitation, talk about reading music and poor light, and the recording is paused.
643.q: You play on music, can you play it by hand? No, I play by notes, you see. You know how to play on song, just want you, you know.

644.t: Introductions and playing tunes for the visitors
644.s: The hosts identify themselves (Bill a trombonist, Raymond a book salesman), then they play tunes, including a Joe Burton number.
644.ch: Tape one: clubs, musicians and old friends
644.q: But I can tell you a lot of things. Yes, sir. Let's play it soon.

309.t: Tape chatter: Dick plays and the interviewers react
309.s: Dick Allen plays something on the blues and the group chats about it.
309.q: What have they done to my song? That's what it meant.
